findings.checklist_item: State the failure-disposition contract per new arm: for a refused admission say whether it is retryable/queued (WAIT_AND_RETRY) vs fatal, and for a container OOM-restart say what in-flight callers surface.
evidence: 'A limit converts "host wedges unpredictably" into "one container restarts, loudly"'
'One admission controller ... an admission is refused'
AC2: 'a named container restarts, an admission is refused ... instead of wedging'
Gates are described as 'queueable' but the plan never states, with a disposition word, what a refused admission surfaces to the gate caller.
findings.finding: W2 and W4 add new failure/degradation arms (a container hitting its memory limit and restarting; an admission being refused by the controller), and AC2 names the observable outcome, but the plan never states the DISPOSITION each arm surfaces to its caller — in particular whether a refused gate admission is retryable/queueable (WAIT_AND_RETRY) or fatal to that gate run.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a 'Failure-disposition contract' note: an admission refused for capacity is retryable/queued (the gate waits and retries, WAIT_AND_RETRY) — never surfaced as a fatal gate failure; a container that hits its memory limit restarts and its in-flight work is re-queued rather than reported as a permanent error.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify W4's mechanism: name the cross-process coordination substrate the unified admission controller uses to observe total/committed memory, and state that admission reserves against each workload's PEAK RSS (not current free memory) so concurrent admits cannot collectively overshoot.
evidence: Plan W4: 'One admission controller aware of total memory, replacing independent gate semaphore + MCP thread limiter + review-bot concurrency, each locally reasonable.'
gate_admission.py gate_admission() is a per-host fcntl slot-file acquired inside the Python gate process (_acquire_slot/_slot_dir), not a cross-container memory arbiter
Plan's own profile: gates are 'BATCH: 15-20 min, ~700 MB' — RSS ramps after admission, so admit-on-free-memory is a TOCTOU against peak
findings.finding: W4's proposed mechanism ('one admission controller aware of total memory, replacing independent gate semaphore + MCP thread limiter + review-bot concurrency') is under-specified in two ways that bear on whether it can work: the three limiters it unifies live in separate processes/containers (the gate semaphore is a single-process, per-host fcntl slot-file in gate_admission.py; MCP thread limiter and review-bot concurrency are elsewhere), so a single controller needs a shared coordination substrate the plan never names; and a memory-aware admit decision is check-then-act — it admits on observed free memory, then the admitted batch workload grows RSS over 15-20 min, so concurrent admissions can collectively overshoot unless the controller reserves against PEAK RSS rather than current free memory.
findings.location: Workstreams — W4 (Bound the SUM, not the parts)
scenarios: Two gates both admitted when memory looks free, then both ramp to ~700 MB peak and jointly cross the line the controller was meant to hold
The controller can only see the process it runs in and cannot actually observe MCP/review-bot RSS, so it bounds a proxy rather than the SUM it claims to bound
findings.suggested_fix: Have W4 reserve against a committed budget: each admitted workload debits its measured PEAK RSS (from W5's telemetry / GATE_PEAK_RSS) from a shared host budget at admit time and credits it back on exit, rather than sampling instantaneous free memory — this closes the admit-then-grow TOCTOU and makes the SUM the controller actually enforces.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State W4's positive rationale relative to W1+W2: explain what a unified memory-aware controller buys once the batch tier is off-host (W1) and every container has a hard mem_limit (W2), or mark W4 as an alternative/contingency rather than an independent workstream.
evidence: Plan W1 removes 'the bursty heavy consumer entirely'; W2 'converts host wedges unpredictably into one container restarts, loudly'
W4 is presented as replacing the gate semaphore among others, but the gate tier it governs is what W1 relocates off-host
No positive rationale in W4 for choosing a unified controller over the simpler W1 (relocate) + W2 (hard limits) combination it structurally overlaps
findings.finding: W4 overlaps W1 and W2 without reconciling them, and carries no positive rationale for why a unified memory-aware controller is needed once those land. If W1 moves the batch gate tier off-host, the gate semaphore no longer competes for this host's RAM; and W2's per-container hard mem_limit already converts overshoot into 'one container restarts, loudly' (AC2). The plan does not state whether W4 is still required after W1+W2, is an alternative to them, or is redundant — leaving the implementer without a rationale for the more complex approach.
findings.location: Workstreams — W4 vs W1/W2; leverage ordering
scenarios: An implementer builds the cross-process controller (highest-complexity item) after W1 has already removed the batch consumer it was chiefly meant to bound
AC1 is read as requiring W4 even though W2's hard limits already 'ENFORCE rather than document' the bound
